expectations.text: At least two separate ILAC blocks (Law and Application parts)
Every Issue is framed as a question ("Whether ..." or ends with ?)
expectations.evidence: 3 issue statements; first: Could the clown caricature, posted online, constitute an offence under s.233(1)(a) CMA as it stood in 2016?

expectations.text: Application is longer than Law in every ILAC block
Discussion has a comparison table with an ICCPR column
Reference list with at least 6 entries
Status of laws flagged (in force / amended / repealed)
Flags the 2025 amendment to s.233 ('grossly offensive')
Application reasons element by element against the facts
expectations.evidence: [blind grader] Issue 1 lists five elements (i)-(v) and applies them: 'Elements (i), (ii) and (v) are not seriously contested... The contest lies in elements (iii) and (iv)'.

expectations.text: Application gives the strongest argument for both sides on contested points
expectations.evidence: [blind grader] 'On one hand, the prosecution would argue... offensive in character... On the other hand, the defence would argue that offensive is undefined... annoyance may be a foreseeable by-product'; similar split on selective enforcement in Issue 2.

expectations.text: Application compares the facts with decided cases (analogises or distinguishes a precedent)
expectations.evidence: [blind grader] Issue 3 compares Fahmi's clown image with Heidy Quah: 'plausibly closer to Quah's protected opinion than to targeted harassment. But a clown image is also more plainly insulting than Quah's factual post, so the analogy is not clean'. Issue 1 has no case comparison.

expectations.text: Every Conclusion answers its Issue directly and states a degree of certainty
expectations.evidence: [blind grader] 'It is likely, and it was in fact held at three court levels'; 'most likely procedurally lawful'; 'open to serious doubt'. Each answers its question with a degree of certainty.

expectations.text: Discussion states where the chosen theory fits AND where it fits poorly
expectations.evidence: [blind grader] Habermas and Siebert are used; 'These theories fit poorly, however. They were built to classify press systems... not individual online satirists... treat Malaysia as a fixed type'. The poor-fit comment is joint rather than per theory.

expectations.text: Discussion explains why each comparator jurisdiction was chosen and links back to the ILAC findings
expectations.evidence: [blind grader] 'Chosen because each has (or had) a near-identical grossly offensive/annoyance offence'; links back: 'Malaysia's Federal Court took a third path... more dependent on prosecutorial and judicial restraint, which was exactly what failed in Fahmi's case'. Also explains why Singapore and Thailand are omitted.

expectations.text: Uncertain or unverified points are flagged rather than stated as fact
expectations.evidence: [blind grader] Separate 'Confirmed' list; 'Source conflicts and gaps' paragraph; '[to verify]' on the date of the Federal Court referral ruling, Najib pardon status and foreign citations.

expectations.text: Explains how s.233 has changed since 2016 and what that means for a similar case today
expectations.evidence: [blind grader] Dated table (2016 wording, 11 Feb 2025 'grossly offensive' and RM500,000/2 years, Court of Appeal 19 Aug 2025, Federal Court 6 Feb 2026) with a net-effect paragraph. Implication for a similar case is less explicit than B's: it sits in Issue 3 ('plausibly closer to Quah's protected opinion') and the conclusion ('depend on how prosecutors and judges apply the law').
